content: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS), which occur during childbirth, are associated with significant maternal complications. These include perineal pain, dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse), and anal incontinence, all of which can result in both psychological and physical consequences. Many women, however, do not seek medical care due to feelings of embarrassment. The two primary surgical techniques for repairing damage to the external anal sphincter (EAS) are the end-to-end (approximation) repair and the overlap repair. The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness of the overlap repair technique versus the end-to-end repair technique in reducing anal incontinence, perineal pain, and dyspareunia, as well as in improving overall quality of life following OASIS. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of September 30, 2013) and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. They included randomized controlled trials that compared different techniques for the immediate primary repair of the EAS following OASIS. The quality of the trials was independently assessed by all authors. Six trials, involving a total of 588 women, were included in the analysis. The quality of these trials varied, and there was significant heterogeneity in the reported outcomes, time points, and results. Meta-analyses revealed no statistically significant differences between the two repair techniques in terms of perineal pain (risk ratio [RR] 0.08, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.00 to 1.45, one trial, 52 women), dyspareunia (average RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.24, two trials, 151 women), or flatus incontinence (average RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.23, three trials, 256 women) at 12 months post-repair. However, the overlap repair technique was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of faecal urgency (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.86, one trial, 52 women) and a lower anal incontinence score (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.70, 95% CI -1.26 to -0.14, one trial, 52 women) compared to the end-to-end repair. Additionally, the overlap technique demonstrated a significantly lower risk of worsening anal incontinence symptoms over a 12-month period (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.79, one trial, 41 women). There was no significant difference in overall quality of life between the two techniques. At 36 months of follow-up, there were no differences between the two techniques in terms of flatus incontinence (average RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.99, one trial, 68 women) or faecal incontinence (average RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.34 to 2.98, one trial, 68 women). In conclusion, the available data suggest that at one year post-repair, the immediate primary overlap repair of the external anal sphincter is associated with a lower risk of faecal urgency and anal incontinence symptoms compared to the end-to-end repair. However, by 36 months, there appears to be no difference between the two techniques in terms of flatus or faecal incontinence. It is important to note that these findings are based on only two small trials, and further research is necessary to confirm or refute these results.
